content: Physical activity provides significant health benefits for adults and older adults living with chronic conditions. For cancer survivors, engaging in physical activity reduces all-cause mortality, cancer-specific mortality, and the risk of cancer recurrence or the development of a second primary cancer. For individuals with hypertension, physical activity improves cardiovascular disease mortality, slows disease progression, enhances physical function, and improves health-related quality of life. For those with type-2 diabetes, physical activity lowers mortality rates from cardiovascular disease and slows disease progression. For individuals living with HIV, physical activity enhances physical fitness and mental health by reducing symptoms of anxiety and depression, without negatively affecting disease progression (e.g., CD4 count and viral load) or body composition. Adults with chronic conditions who cannot meet the recommended levels of physical activity should aim to engage in activity according to their abilities. They should start with small amounts of physical activity and gradually increase the frequency, intensity, and duration over time. Consulting a physical activity specialist or healthcare professional is advised to tailor activity types and amounts to individual needs, abilities, functional limitations, medications, and overall treatment plans. Pre-exercise medical clearance is generally unnecessary for individuals without contraindications when beginning lightor moderate-intensity physical activity, such as brisk walking or daily living activities. Higher levels of sedentary behavior in adults, including cancer survivors and individuals with hypertension, type-2 diabetes, or HIV, are associated with poor health outcomes, such as increased all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, and the incidence of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and type-2 diabetes. Adults and older adults with chronic conditions should limit sedentary time and replace it with physical activity of any intensity, including light-intensity activity, to gain health benefits. To mitigate the harmful effects of high sedentary behavior, they should aim to exceed the recommended levels of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity. For substantial health benefits, adults with chronic conditions should engage in at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or an equivalent combination of moderateand vigorous-intensity activity throughout the week. For additional health benefits, they may increase moderate-intensity aerobic activity to more than 300 minutes per week or vigorous-intensity aerobic activity to more than 150 minutes per week. Older adults should also include multicomponent physical activities that emphasize functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity on three or more days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. Additionally, muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups should be performed at moderate or greater intensity on two or more days per week for added health benefits. For children and adolescents (aged 5–17 years) living with disabilities, physical activity offers many of the same health benefits as for their peers without disabilities. Engaging in some physical activity is better than none. If they cannot meet the recommended levels, any amount of physical activity will still provide health benefits. They should start with small amounts of activity and gradually increase the frequency, intensity, and duration over time. There are no significant risks associated with appropriate physical activity for children and adolescents with disabilities, provided it aligns with their current activity level, health status, and physical function. The health benefits of physical activity outweigh the risks. Children and adolescents with disabilities should limit sedentary time, particularly recreational screen time, as higher amounts of sedentary behavior are linked to increased adiposity, poorer cardiometabolic health, reduced fitness, behavioral issues, and shorter sleep duration. They should aim for an average of at least 60 minutes per day of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity, mostly aerobic, across the week. Vigorous-intensity aerobic activities and those that strengthen muscles and bones should be included at least three days per week. For adults living with disabilities, physical activity provides additional health benefits. For individuals with multiple sclerosis, it improves physical function and health-related quality of life across physical, mental, and social domains. For those with spinal cord injuries, it enhances walking function, muscular strength, upper extremity function, and health-related quality of life. For individuals with cognitive impairments, such as Parkinson’s disease or a history of stroke, physical activity improves physical function, cognition, and quality of life. It may also benefit adults with schizophrenia by improving cognition and quality of life. For adults with intellectual disabilities, physical activity enhances physical function, and for those with major clinical depression, it improves quality of life. In summary, regular physical activity is strongly recommended for individuals with chronic conditions or disabilities, as it provides substantial health benefits and outweighs the risks associated with sedentary behavior.
